name: Bundeli
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Jaiswal, Mahesh P. 1962. A linguistic study of Bundeli (a dialect of Madhyadesa). Brill, xii+174pp. Not found on archive.org or elsewhere online.

new_statements.quote: Stress accent in Bundeli is irregular and fluctuates occasionally in every word. […] all the main rules of stress accent in Bundeli are similar to those in Hindi and its other dialects. […] (i) Due to the mutation of the final vowel when a word or a syllable, from the point of view of pronunciation, has a consonantal ending the stress is on the penultimate vowel, for instance, kā́gaja "paper"; sáṛaka "road". (ii) In a word of one or more conjunct consonants the stress is on the vowel immediately before the conjunct consonant […] In words of two, three or four syllables the stress is usually on the last or the last but one, if it happens to be longer than the other.
new_statements.citation: Jaiswal, Mahesh Prasad. 1962. A Linguistic Study of Bundeli (a dialect of Madhyadesa). Orientalia Rheno-Traiectina VIII. Leiden: E. J. Brill.
new_statements.locator: Ch. I Phonology, section 'Accentuation, Stress', subsection 'Stress accent in Bundeli', pp. 28-29 (PDF pages 40-41 of the DLI scan; page renders saved)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is weak, irregular and fluctuating, and follows the Hindi rules (Guru, Hindi Vyakaran §56): in a word that ends in a consonant in pronunciation, stress is on the penultimate vowel (kā́gaja 'paper', sáṛaka 'road'); before a consonant cluster, stress is on the vowel immediately preceding the cluster (bháddō, rássī, bíddyā); the long ā of causative stems is always stressed (karā́nō, likhā́nō, baiṭhā́nō); in words of two to four syllables stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable, whichever is longer (pā́cīsa, bhā́va, kudā́rī; camārā́na, maṭákā, dēkhabṓ, sakā́rē; sirahā́nō, barasā́tī, pichavāṛṓ). Net: stress on the heaviest of the last two syllables, near the right edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Bundeli (a 'secondary stress on the first syllable' is mentioned only for the reconstructed MIA accent, p. 28).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic words 'usually have no stress unless they are used in a sentence'; stress is 'irregular and fluctuates occasionally in every word' and is 'sometimes difficult to distinguish' from emphasis; a few pairs are distinguished by accent alone: liyē 'having taken' vs (kē)lié 'for', kí 'did' vs kī 'of'. The author says the rules are those of Hindi 'some of which are also valid for Bundeli' and prefers illustration to description.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolated citation forms (examples are single words with acute accent marks); monosyllables receive stress only in sentence context. Stress is explicitly called weak and unstable; the reading 'weight-sensitive' is the best fit of the rules given, but the source itself frames the system as irregular.
new_statements.identity_note: Jaiswal 1962 explicitly describes 'standard Bundeli' of central Bundelkhand (whole districts of Tikamgarh, Sagar, Jhansi, most of Jalaun and Hamirpur, parts of Gwalior, Bhopal and Datia; Introduction pp. 9-10), i.e. the language-level bund1253 itself, not a peripheral variety. Ahirwal 2011 (silent on stress) describes the Bundeli of Chittorgarh, Kota and Bundi districts in Rajasthan.

sources.note: Ch. I Phonology has a section 'Accentuation, Stress' (pp. 27-30) with a subsection 'Stress accent in Bundeli' (pp. 28-29): stress is weak, irregular and fluctuating; main rules as in Hindi (Guru, Hindi Vyakaran §56): penultimate vowel in consonant-final words, vowel before a conjunct consonant, long a of causatives always stressed; monosyllables unstressed in isolation; in 2-4-syllable words stress on the last or the last-but-one, whichever is longer; a few accent-distinguished pairs (liye/lie, ki/ki). Examples given with acute accent marks. No secondary stress mentioned for Bundeli.

sources.note: Phonology pp. 328-335 lists 45 segmental + 2 suprasegmental phonemes; §2.1.2 'Co-articulated features or suprasegmental phonemes' covers only nasalisation (and length); §2.4 syllable structure (max. four syllables). Nothing on stress or accent. Describes Bundeli of Chittorgarh, Kota and Bundi districts, Rajasthan.
Phonology section is a consonant chart only; nothing on stress. Its reference list pointed to the archive.org DLI copy of Jaiswal 1962 (item in.ernet.dli.2015.262193) and to Boehm 2015.

sources.citation: Agrawal, Rameshwar Prasad. 1963. Bundeli ka bhashashastriya adhyayan [A linguistic study of Bundeli] (in Hindi). Seth Bholaram Seksaria Smarak Granthmala. Lucknow: Lucknow University Hindi Prakashan. (Published form of the 1959 Lucknow PhD 'The descriptive analysis of Bundeli' listed in Glottolog.)
sources.note: Phonology chapter (dhvani-vichar) treats vowels, consonants, syllable division (akshar-vitaran §28, defining the syllable as a breath-pulse unit) and juncture (shabd-sangam §29), then passes to morphology; no word-stress section found. balaghat ('stress') occurs only in the syntax chapter (interrogative words carry stress; any word can be stressed for emphasis) and svaraghat for interjections; word-order inversion 'indicates emphasis'. scanned-based reading; the term balaghat OCRs correctly where it occurs, so the absence is probably real.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.). 1916. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX Part I: Indo-Aryan family, Central group: Western Hindi and Panjabi. Calcutta. Bundeli section (pp. 91 ff.).
sources.note: The Bundeli grammar sketch's 'Pronunciation' paragraph covers vowel shortening, ai/au, r/r, h-elision; nothing on stress or accent. The volume's only 'accented syllable' remarks are in the Hindostani (Dakhini, Upper Doab) and Panjabi sections.
